title: 5.1 Point estimates and sampling variability
outcomes: Tell a parameter ($p$) from a point estimate ($\hat{p}$), and sampling error from bias.
Explain what a sampling distribution is, and why a bigger sample makes it narrower.
Compute the standard error of $\hat{p}$, plugging in $\hat{p}$ when $p$ is unknown.
Check the conditions for modelling $\hat{p}$ with a normal distribution.

modules.title: Parameter and point estimate
modules.reading:
Pollsters want to know about a whole **population**, for example the share of all American adults who support more solar energy. That share is the **parameter**, written $p$. Nobody knows $p$ exactly, because nobody asks everyone.

Instead, a poll asks a **sample** of $n$ people, where $n$ is the **sample size**. The share of the sample who say yes is the **sample proportion**, written $\hat{p}$ ("p-hat"). We use $\hat{p}$ as a **point estimate** of $p$: our single best guess.

check.prompt: A poll of $n = 1000$ adults finds that 45% approve of the president. Which statement is right?

options.text: $p = 0.45$, because that's what the poll found
$\hat{p} = 0.45$, and so $p$ must be very close to 0.45

misconception.text: Treats the number computed from the sample as the population parameter itself.

reExplanation.text: $p$ belongs to the whole population, so only asking everyone would give it. 0.45 came from 1,000 people, so it's the sample proportion $\hat{p}$. The hat marks a number computed from a sample.

misconception.text: Expects a sample statistic to land very close to the parameter, underestimating sampling variability.

source.reference: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1971). Belief in the law of small numbers. Psychological Bulletin, 76(2), 105-110.

reExplanation.text: $\hat{p} = 0.45$ is right, but the second half goes too far. Another random 1,000 people would give a slightly different share. How far $\hat{p}$ tends to land from $p$ is what the rest of this lesson measures, so we can't assume "very close" yet.
Ask two questions: is the number from everyone or from a sample? And is it known exactly, or a guess?

alternatives.prompt: In the notation of this section, what does $n$ stand for?

options.text: The number of people in the sample
The number of people in the population
The number of people who said yes

misconception.text: Mixes up the sample size with the population size.

source.reference: delMas, R., Garfield, J., Ooms, A., & Chance, B. (2007). Assessing students' conceptual understanding after a first course in statistics. Statistics Education Research Journal, 6(2), 28-58.

reExplanation.text: $n$ counts the people actually asked. In a poll of 1,000 adults, $n = 1000$ whether the country has 1 million or 250 million adults.

misconception.text: Confuses the sample size with the count of successes.

reExplanation.text: The count of people who said yes is usually called $x$. The sample size $n$ counts everyone who was asked, so $\hat{p} = x / n$.
$n$ is the sample size: how many people the poll asked.

alternatives.explanation: $n$ is the sample size: the number of people the poll actually asked. The population's size is a different number, and the count of yeses is $x$.

check.explanation: 0.45 was computed from the 1,000 people in the poll, so it's $\hat{p}$. It's our estimate of $p$, the share among everyone, which stays unknown. How close the two are is what standard error will tell us.

modules.title: Two kinds of error
modules.reading:
The **error** in an estimate is the gap between $\hat{p}$ and $p$. It has two parts.

**Sampling error** is the luck of the draw: one random sample comes out a bit high, another a bit low. It shrinks as the sample size $n$ grows.

**Bias** is a tendency to miss in the same direction every time, for example because of how a question is worded or who gets asked. A bigger sample doesn't fix bias. Careful data collection does.

check.prompt: Sort each problem by the kind of error it causes.

categories.label: Sampling error (a bigger sample shrinks it)
Bias (a bigger sample won't fix it)

items.text: The question asks "Don't you agree the stadium is a great idea?"
A survey about exercise asks only people at a gym
Two random polls of 100 people give 0.86 and 0.91
A random sample of 50 happens to include more students than usual

check.explanation: Bias pushes every sample the same way, so asking more people only gives a more precise wrong answer. Sampling error is the luck of the draw, which averages out as the sample grows.

misconception.text: Treats a systematic error from question wording as sampling error that a bigger sample would remove.

reExplanation.text: A leading question nudges every respondent toward yes, in every sample. Ask 10,000 people instead of 100 and you get a very precise estimate of the wrong number. That's bias.

check.prompt: If every sample tends to come out too high, will a bigger sample fix it?

misconception.text: Believes a large enough sample cancels out who was chosen, even when the choosing isn't random.

reExplanation.text: People at a gym exercise more than most people, and every gym sample has that lean. More gym-goers won't add the people who never go.
Ask of each problem: would it still be there if we asked 10 times as many people the same way? If yes, it's bias. If it would shrink, it's sampling error.

alternatives.prompt: A student poll asks: "Do you support your school by supporting funding for the new stadium?" What kind of error is the wording most likely to cause?

options.text: Sampling error, which asking more students would fix
Bias, pushing the estimate up however many students are asked
No error, as long as the students are picked at random

misconception.text: Treats a systematic error from question wording as sampling error that a bigger sample would remove.

reExplanation.text: The wording nudges every respondent toward "yes", so the poll overestimates support in every sample. Asking 10,000 students instead of 100 would just give a very precise wrong answer. That's bias.

check.prompt: If every sample tends to come out too high, will a bigger sample fix it?

misconception.text: Believes random selection alone guarantees an unbiased estimate, ignoring measurement problems such as leading questions.

reExplanation.text: Random selection protects against one source of bias: who gets asked. It does nothing about **what** they're asked. A leading question biases the answers even from a perfectly random sample.
Ask: does the problem push the answer the same way every time (bias), or does it vary by luck from sample to sample (sampling error)?

alternatives.explanation: The wording leans every respondent toward yes, so every sample overestimates support. That's bias. Asking more students the same leading question only makes the wrong answer more precise.

alternatives.prompt: Which change reduces sampling error but leaves bias unchanged?

options.text: Asking more people in the same way

misconception.text: Mixes up the fixes for bias and for sampling error.

reExplanation.text: Rewording fixes bias, the push in one direction. Sampling error shrinks with sample size.
Sampling error depends on how many are asked. Bias depends on how they're asked and who.

alternatives.explanation: Sampling error comes from the luck of who's in the sample, so asking more people shrinks it. Bias comes from how or whom we ask, and asking more people the same way keeps it.

modules.title: The sampling distribution
modules.reading:
Suppose we knew $p = 0.88$ and simulated polls of $n = 1000$ on a computer. One poll gives $\hat{p} = 0.894$, the next $0.885$, the next $0.878$. Repeat 10,000 times and draw a histogram of all the $\hat{p}$ values. That histogram is the **sampling distribution** of $\hat{p}$: how $\hat{p}$ varies from sample to sample.

Its **center** is at $p$ (0.88), its **spread** is small, and its **shape** is symmetric and bell-like.

In real life we only ever see one sample, never this histogram. But it's what tells us how far to trust that one $\hat{p}$.

check.prompt: A poll asks 1,000 adults a yes/no question. What is the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$?

options.text: The 1,000 yes and no answers from that poll
The $\hat{p}$ values you'd get from many different random samples of 1,000
The answers every adult in the population would give

misconception.text: Thinks the distribution of the data in one sample is the sampling distribution.

source.reference: Castro Sotos, A. E., Vanhoof, S., Van den Noortgate, W., & Onghena, P. (2007). Students' misconceptions of statistical inference: A review of the empirical evidence from research on statistics education. Educational Research Review, 2(2), 98-113.

reExplanation.text: The 1,000 answers are the data from **one** sample, and they give **one** $\hat{p}$. The sampling distribution is one level up: imagine many polls, each giving its own $\hat{p}$, and look at how those $\hat{p}$ values spread out.

check.prompt: Each point in the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ is...

misconception.text: Thinks the sampling distribution is (or looks like) the population distribution.

source.reference: Castro Sotos, A. E., Vanhoof, S., Van den Noortgate, W., & Onghena, P. (2007). Students' misconceptions of statistical inference: A review of the empirical evidence from research on statistics education. Educational Research Review, 2(2), 98-113.

reExplanation.text: Everyone's answers make up the population, which is just yes and no in some share. The sampling distribution is about a statistic: many $\hat{p}$ values, one per imagined sample. It's centered at $p$ but much narrower than the yes/no spread of the population.
Think of the simulation in the reading: run many polls, keep each poll's $\hat{p}$, and make a histogram of those numbers.

alternatives.prompt: If we simulate many polls with $p = 0.88$ and $n = 1000$, where is the center of the histogram of $\hat{p}$ values?

misconception.text: Anchors on a single sample's result as if it were the center of the sampling distribution.

reExplanation.text: One poll can land a little high or low. Across thousands of random polls, those misses balance out, and the $\hat{p}$ values center on the true $p$.
Random samples don't lean either way, so their $\hat{p}$ values gather around the true $p$.

alternatives.explanation: Random samples don't lean either way, so their $\hat{p}$ values average out to the true $p = 0.88$. That's why the histogram is centered there.

check.explanation: Each sample gives one $\hat{p}$. The sampling distribution is the pattern of all the $\hat{p}$ values you'd get from many random samples of the same size: how much $\hat{p}$ varies from poll to poll.

explore.why: The student changes the sample size and sees the histogram of p-hat narrow around p. It targets the belief that a bigger sample moves the estimate, or that sample size doesn't matter.
explore.prompt: A population where 88% say yes ($p = 0.88$). Pick a sample size, draw 1,000 samples, and look at where their $\hat{p}$ values land. Then pick another size and draw again.

prediction.prompt: If each sample has 1,000 people instead of 10, the $\hat{p}$ values will…

explore.thinkAbout: Picture one poll of 10 people and one of 1,000. One unusual person moves the first poll's $\hat{p}$ by 0.1, and the second's by 0.001. Which poll can land far from 0.88?
explore.notice: Each bar counts the samples that gave that $\hat{p}$. With $n = 10$ they range widely; with $n = 1000$ they pile up near 0.88. The center stays at $p$ either way: a bigger sample makes $\hat{p}$ more precise, it doesn't move it.

modules.title: Standard error
modules.reading:
The spread of the sampling distribution has a name: the **standard error** of $\hat{p}$, written $SE_{\hat{p}}$. It's roughly how far a typical $\hat{p}$ lands from $p$.

$$SE_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$$

Here $p$ is the population proportion (as a proportion like 0.88, never a percent like 88), $1 - p$ is the share who say no, and $n$ is the sample size. For $p = 0.88$ and $n = 1000$ the formula gives 0.010, which matches the simulation's spread.

check.prompt: Use $SE_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ with $p = 0.88$ and $n = 1000$. Give three decimal places.

misconception.text: Forgets the square root in the standard error formula.

reExplanation.text: $0.88 \times 0.12 / 1000 = 0.0001056$ is the part **under** the square root. Take its square root to get the standard error.

misconception.text: Leaves out the $(1-p)$ factor.

reExplanation.text: The top of the fraction is $p(1-p)$: the yes share times the no share, here $0.88 \times 0.12$.

misconception.text: Uses percentages (88 and 12) in a formula written for proportions.

reExplanation.text: The formula needs proportions: $p = 0.88$, not 88. With percentages the answer comes out about 100 times too big.
Work in steps: $1 - p = 0.12$, then $p(1-p)$, then divide by $n$, then take the square root.

alternatives.prompt: With $p = 0.5$ and $n = 100$, what is $SE_{\hat{p}}$? Give two decimal places.

misconception.text: Forgets the square root in the standard error formula.

reExplanation.text: $0.5 \times 0.5 / 100 = 0.0025$ is under the square root. $\sqrt{0.0025} = 0.05$.
$p(1-p) = 0.25$; divide by 100; take the square root.

alternatives.explanation: $0.5 \times 0.5 / 100 = 0.0025$, and $\sqrt{0.0025} = 0.05$. With only 100 people, a typical $\hat{p}$ is about 5 percentage points from $p$.

check.explanation: $0.88 \times 0.12 = 0.1056$; divided by 1000 gives $0.0001056$; the square root is about 0.010. So a typical $\hat{p}$ from these polls lands about 1 percentage point from $p$.

modules.title: Bigger samples, smaller error
modules.reading:
Look at where the sample size $n$ sits in $SE_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$: in the bottom of the fraction. A bigger $n$ makes the standard error smaller, so $\hat{p}$ values bunch more tightly around $p$.

This matches intuition: more data tends to give a more precise estimate. Because of the square root, though, the gain is slow. Four times the sample only halves the standard error.

check.prompt: Two pollsters estimate the same $p$. One asks $n = 50$ people, the other $n = 1000$. Whose $\hat{p}$ is more likely to be far from $p$?

options.text: Neither: both are random samples, so they're equally likely to be off

misconception.text: Thinks a larger sample gives a more spread-out sampling distribution.

source.reference: delMas, R. C., Garfield, J., & Chance, B. L. (1999). A model of classroom research in action: Developing simulation activities to improve students' statistical reasoning. Journal of Statistics Education, 7(3).

reExplanation.text: A bigger sample captures more of the population's variety, but $\hat{p}$ is an **average** over the sample. Averaging over more people smooths out the luck, so the sampling distribution gets **narrower** as $n$ grows: $n$ is in the denominator of the SE.

check.prompt: If $n$ goes up, does $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ go up or down?

misconception.text: Thinks small and large samples are equally likely to give a statistic far from the parameter.

source.reference: Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1972). Subjective probability: A judgment of representativeness. Cognitive Psychology, 3(3), 430-454.

reExplanation.text: Both are random, so neither is biased. But a sample of 50 is much more at the mercy of luck: a handful of unusual people moves $\hat{p}$ a lot. With 1,000 people, the same handful barely matters. The SE formula says it too: $\sqrt{p(1-p)/50}$ is larger than $\sqrt{p(1-p)/1000}$.
Compare the formula for both sample sizes, keeping $p$ the same.

alternatives.prompt: A poll grows from $n = 1000$ to $n = 4000$. What happens to the standard error?

misconception.text: Believes the standard error shrinks in proportion to $1/n$ rather than $1/\sqrt{n}$.

reExplanation.text: $n$ is inside a square root. Multiplying $n$ by 4 multiplies $\sqrt{n}$ by 2, so the SE is divided by 2.
Try the formula with $n = 1000$, then $n = 4000$.

alternatives.explanation: $n$ is inside a square root. Four times the sample multiplies $\sqrt{n}$ by 2, so the SE is divided by 2.

check.explanation: With $n = 50$ the SE is $\sqrt{p(1-p)/50}$, which is larger than $\sqrt{p(1-p)/1000}$. A small sample is more at the mercy of who happens to be in it, so its $\hat{p}$ is more likely to land far from $p$.

explore.why: The student changes n in the standard error formula and sees that four times the sample only halves the error. It targets the belief that the error shrinks in proportion to n.
explore.prompt: This computes $SE_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$. Change $n$ and watch the standard error and the curve.

prediction.prompt: Going from $n = 100$ to $n = 400$ (four times the people), the standard error…

options.text: becomes a quarter of what it was

explore.thinkAbout: $n$ sits inside a square root. If $n$ is four times bigger, what happens to $\sqrt{n}$?
explore.notice: From 100 to 400 the standard error halves, and from 400 to 1600 it halves again. The curve flattens: each extra person helps less than the one before.

modules.title: The Central Limit Theorem
modules.reading:
The bell shape in the simulation isn't luck. The **Central Limit Theorem** says: when the observations are **independent** and the sample is large enough, $\hat{p}$ follows a normal distribution with mean $p$ and standard error $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$.

"Large enough" has a rule of thumb, the **success-failure condition**: $np \ge 10$ and $n(1-p) \ge 10$. Here $np$ is the expected number of yeses in the sample and $n(1-p)$ the expected number of nos. Both need to be at least 10.

check.prompt: A sample has $n = 10$ and $p = 0.25$. Can we model $\hat{p}$ with a normal distribution?

options.text: Yes: the sample is random, so the Central Limit Theorem applies

misconception.text: Believes independence alone is enough for the Central Limit Theorem, forgetting the sample-size condition.

reExplanation.text: The theorem has **two** conditions: independence **and** a large enough sample. A random sample of 10 meets the first but not the second: with $np = 2.5$ we expect only 2 or 3 yeses, and the distribution of $\hat{p}$ comes out lumpy and skewed.

misconception.text: Treats the success-failure threshold as approximate and checks only one of the two products.

reExplanation.text: Both products must reach 10, and here neither does: $np = 2.5$ and $n(1-p) = 7.5$. With so few expected yeses, $\hat{p}$ can only take values like 0, 0.1, 0.2, and the histogram is skewed, not bell-shaped.
Compute both $np$ and $n(1-p)$ and compare each with 10.

alternatives.prompt: For $n = 1000$ and $p = 0.88$, what is $n(1-p)$, the expected number of nos?

misconception.text: Computes $np$ when asked for $n(1-p)$.

reExplanation.text: $np = 880$ is the expected number of yeses. The nos are $n(1-p) = 1000 \times 0.12$.
$1 - p = 0.12$, then multiply by $n = 1000$.

alternatives.explanation: $n(1-p) = 1000 \times 0.12 = 120$ expected nos. Together with $np = 880$ expected yeses, both are well above 10, so the normal model works.

check.explanation: The success-failure condition needs both $np$ and $n(1-p)$ to be at least 10. Here $np = 10 \times 0.25 = 2.5$, so we expect only 2 or 3 yeses per sample, and the distribution of $\hat{p}$ is lumpy and skewed, not normal.

modules.title: Checking independence
modules.reading:
The other condition is **independence**: one person's answer shouldn't affect another's. The usual way to get it is a **simple random sample** of the population, or random assignment in an experiment. For other sampling, like items pulled now and then from a production line, you have to use judgement.

Some books add that the sample should be at most 10% of the population. This isn't a warning against big samples. Past 10%, the sample covers so much of the population that $\hat{p}$ can't stray far from $p$, and the formula $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ overstates the error. Your estimate is then better than the formula says, so this check is optional.

check.prompt: A random sample of 400 students is taken from a campus of 5,000 students. Is the sample too small a share of the campus to estimate $p$?

options.text: No. Randomness and the sample size are what matter, and 400 is under 10% of 5,000
Yes. 400 is only 8% of the campus, so it can't represent it
Yes. A sample should include at least half the population

misconception.text: Thinks a sample is only trustworthy if it is a large fraction of the population.

source.reference: delMas, R., Garfield, J., Ooms, A., & Chance, B. (2007). Assessing students' conceptual understanding after a first course in statistics. Statistics Education Research Journal, 6(2), 28-58.

reExplanation.text: How precise $\hat{p}$ is depends on $n$, the number asked, not on what share of the population they are. The SE formula has no population size in it. The only share rule runs the other way: the sample should be **at most** 10% of the population.

check.prompt: Does the population's size appear in $SE_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$?

misconception.text: Thinks a sample is only trustworthy if it is a large fraction of the population.

source.reference: delMas, R., Garfield, J., Ooms, A., & Chance, B. (2007). Assessing students' conceptual understanding after a first course in statistics. Statistics Education Research Journal, 6(2), 28-58.

reExplanation.text: National polls ask about 1,000 people out of hundreds of millions, far less than half, and still estimate well. A random sample's precision comes from $n$, not from covering the population.
Look at what's in the standard error formula, and at which way the 10% rule points.

alternatives.prompt: Which sample is most likely to give independent observations?

options.text: A simple random sample of the town's voters
People who chose to answer an online poll

misconception.text: Treats a volunteer sample as if it were random.

reExplanation.text: People who choose to answer are self-selected, and often share strong opinions. A simple random sample gives everyone the same chance of being asked.
Independence usually comes from random selection.

alternatives.explanation: In a simple random sample everyone has the same chance of being asked, and one person's answer doesn't affect another's. Volunteers and friends are chosen in ways that link their answers.

check.explanation: Precision comes from $n$, the number asked, and from random sampling. 400 is 8% of 5,000, which also meets the rule that a sample should be at most 10% of the population.

modules.title: The plug-in principle
modules.reading:
In real polls we don't know $p$, which is the reason for polling. So we can't put $p$ into the formulas. Instead we **plug in** $\hat{p}$, the proportion from our sample.

For the success-failure condition we check $n\hat{p} \ge 10$ and $n(1-\hat{p}) \ge 10$, and for the standard error we use $$SE_{\hat{p}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$$

This is called the **substitution approximation** or **plug-in principle**. The answer barely changes for a nearby $p$, so it works well.

check.prompt: A random sample of $n = 400$ adults finds that 120 say yes. Estimate the standard error of $\hat{p}$ by plugging in $\hat{p}$. Give three decimal places.

misconception.text: Forgets the square root in the standard error formula.

reExplanation.text: $\hat{p} = 120/400 = 0.30$, and $0.30 \times 0.70 / 400 = 0.000525$. That's under the square root. Take the square root.

misconception.text: Uses percentages (30 and 70) in a formula written for proportions.

reExplanation.text: Use proportions: $\hat{p} = 0.30$ and $1 - \hat{p} = 0.70$, not 30 and 70.

misconception.text: Multiplies by the sample size instead of dividing by it.

reExplanation.text: $n$ goes in the bottom: $\sqrt{0.30 \times 0.70 / 400}$. Dividing is what makes the SE shrink for bigger samples.
First $\hat{p} = 120/400$. Then $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$, divide by 400, and take the square root.

alternatives.prompt: Why do we plug $\hat{p}$ into the standard error formula instead of $p$?

options.text: Because $\hat{p}$ is always exactly equal to $p$
Because it makes the standard error smaller

misconception.text: Expects a sample statistic to land very close to the parameter, underestimating sampling variability.

source.reference: Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1971). Belief in the law of small numbers. Psychological Bulletin, 76(2), 105-110.

reExplanation.text: $\hat{p}$ is usually a little off from $p$. We use it because it's the best number we have, and the standard error barely changes for a nearby value.
Ask: which of $p$ and $\hat{p}$ do we actually know after a poll?

alternatives.explanation: After a poll we know $\hat{p}$ but not $p$, which is why we polled. $\hat{p}$ is close enough that the SE barely changes.

check.explanation: $\hat{p} = 120/400 = 0.30$. Then $0.30 \times 0.70 / 400 = 0.000525$, and its square root is about 0.023. We plug in $\hat{p}$ because $p$ is unknown.

modules.title: How p and n shape the distribution
modules.reading:
Simulating many combinations of $p$ and $n$ shows three patterns.

The sampling distribution is always **centered at $p$**, so $\hat{p}$ is **unbiased** when the data are independent.

For a fixed $p$, its **spread shrinks as $n$ grows**. When $np$ or $n(1-p)$ is small, it's also lumpy and skewed; when both are large, it looks normal.

For a fixed $n$, the spread is **largest when $p = 0.5$**, because $p(1-p)$ is largest there.

check.prompt: With $n = 100$ in every case, which population proportion gives the largest standard error for $\hat{p}$?

options.text: They're all the same, since $n$ is the same

misconception.text: Thinks a larger $p$ means more variability in $\hat{p}$.

reExplanation.text: The spread depends on $p(1-p)$, not $p$ alone. For $p = 0.9$, $p(1-p) = 0.09$; for $p = 0.5$ it's 0.25, the largest it can be.

misconception.text: Thinks the standard error depends only on the sample size, ignoring $p$.

reExplanation.text: $n$ matters, but so does $p$: it appears as $p(1-p)$ on top of the fraction. Close to 0 or 1, almost everyone answers the same way, so samples agree more.
Compute $p(1-p)$ for each option and see which is largest.

alternatives.prompt: When the data are independent, where is the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ centered?

misconception.text: Confuses the center of the sampling distribution with its shape, thinking small samples are biased.

reExplanation.text: Sample size changes the spread and the shape, not the center. Even for small $n$, the $\hat{p}$ values average out to $p$: that's what unbiased means.
Center, spread and shape behave differently: only the spread and shape depend on $n$.

alternatives.explanation: Sample size changes the spread and the shape, not the center. Random samples of any size give $\hat{p}$ values that average out to $p$, which is what unbiased means.

check.explanation: The SE depends on $p(1-p)$. That product is 0.09 for $p = 0.1$ or $0.9$, and 0.25 for $p = 0.5$, its largest value. When answers are split evenly, samples disagree the most.

modules.title: Takeaways
modules.reading:
A **point estimate** like $\hat{p} = x/n$ comes from a sample and estimates a **parameter** like $p$. Its error has two parts: sampling error, which a bigger sample shrinks, and bias, which it doesn't.

Across many samples, $\hat{p}$ forms a **sampling distribution** centered at $p$ with standard error $\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$. With independent observations and at least 10 expected yeses and nos, it's approximately normal. In practice we plug in $\hat{p}$ for $p$.

The same idea works for other statistics, such as a sample mean $\bar{x}$ estimating a population mean $\mu$.
